title: FDE First Principles
about: A project-based path from software architect to first-principles AI engineer for the Forward Deployed Engineer role. A topic drops in the morning and gets one to three mornings, depending on its size: you learn it, build it and explain it on video. Each project ends with an article on rajc.work. Maths appears only when a project needs it. About 128 hours of work: at 8 hours a week, plan on 4 to 5 months.

projects.title: Measure before you believe
projects.goal: Build one customer-support assistant three ways (rules, one model call, an agent loop), measure all three, and recommend one with evidence.
projects.math: fractions and averages, error bars, percentiles

projects.title: Meaning as numbers
projects.goal: Build semantic search from scratch with NumPy, measure it, and plug it into project 1.
projects.math: vectors, length, dot product, cosine similarity, matrix × vector

projects.title: Learn a formula from data
projects.goal: Let the computer find your hosting-cost formula, then a yes/no classifier, by gradient descent.
projects.math: lines and slopes, loss, derivatives, gradient descent, overfitting, sigmoid

projects.title: Backprop by hand (micrograd)
projects.goal: Build a tiny autograd engine and neural-net library, then train it.

projects.title: Tiny GPT
projects.goal: Go from counting letters to a small Transformer that writes Shakespeare-like text.
projects.math: probability, logarithms, softmax, matrix multiplication, attention

projects.title: Back to the customer
projects.goal: Explain project 1's failures from first principles, check them against a stronger model, harden the agent, and make the final recommendation like an FDE.
projects.math: paired differences; everything else you reuse

topics.title: One model call: tokens, time and randomness
topics.question: What does one model call really cost in tokens and seconds, and why does the same prompt give different answers?
topics.why: Every agent framework hides this one request. Its token counts are your cost, its seconds are your latency and its randomness is your consistency problem: the three numbers every project here measures.
setup: Ollama is already on your Mac. Pull a small model: `ollama pull qwen3:4b` (8 GB Mac: `ollama pull llama3.2:3b` and change MODEL in the notebook).
In your fde-first-principles folder run `uv sync` once. In VS Code, open the notebook and pick the `.venv` kernel.

learn.title: Ollama API: generate a chat message
learn.how: Read the request body and the response fields. Note which numbers are tokens and which are nanoseconds.

learn.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (Andrej Karpathy): chapter 'inference'
learn.how: Watch 26:01 to 31:09: why the same prompt gives different answers.

build: Send one POST request to http://localhost:11434/api/chat with the `requests` library (no SDK) and `stream: false`.
Print the whole JSON response. Find the reply text, prompt_eval_count, eval_count and total_duration.
Turn total_duration (nanoseconds) into seconds. Compute tokens per second.
Send the same request 5 times with temperature 0.8, then 5 times with temperature 0 and a seed. Compare the answers.
done_when: The notebook runs top to bottom without errors.
It prints tokens in, tokens out and seconds for one call.
It shows the 5 answers at temperature 0.8 and the 5 at temperature 0.
README.md explains, in your words, why the answers differ.
topics.minimum: One raw HTTP call with tokens and seconds printed.
record: Show the raw JSON. Point to the reply, the token counts and the time.
Show the 5 different answers and say why they differ.
Say what this means for a customer who wants 'the same answer every time'.
Two takes at most, then upload to YouTube as Unlisted and paste the link.

Two takes at most, then upload to YouTube as Unlisted and paste the link.

topics.question: How will you know the system works, before you build it?
topics.why: Evals are the contract between you and the customer. Writing them first turns 'it feels good' into numbers. Size matters too: on 30 cases a measured 80% could really be anything from 65% to 95%; on 50 cases the range shrinks to about ± 11 points (day 7 shows why).

learn.how: Read 'Motivation' and 'Level 1: Unit Tests' (steps 1 to 3). Skim the rest.

math.plain: A proportion is a count divided by the total. 6 billing cases out of 30 is 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2 = 20%.

Load and validate every case, then draw a bar chart of cases per intent. Fix every case that fails validation.

topics.title: Why 30 test cases can lie: error bars
topics.question: How big must a difference be before you believe it?
topics.why: Customers will ask 'is the new version better?'. With small test sets the honest answer is often 'we can't tell yet'.

learn.title: A statistical approach to model evaluations (Anthropic)
learn.how: Read the introduction and Recommendation #1 only. Don't worry about the formulas: today's notebook builds them by simulation.

learn.title: Seeing Theory: Basic probability (Brown University)
learn.how: Play with the coin flips. How often do 10 fair flips give 7 or more heads?

math.plain: If a system is right with probability p, a test of n cases wobbles by about √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n). About 95% of the time the truth is within 2 wobbles of what you measured.

build: Simulate a system that is truly 80% right, tested on 30 cases, 10,000 times. Plot the measured accuracies.
From the simulation: how often does a 30-case test show 70% or less?
Write se(p, n). Check that it matches the spread you simulated.
Draw A and B with ± 2 × se error bars. Do they overlap?
Work out the ± range for 30, 50 and 100 cases and for your own test set. How much does each extra case buy?
How many cases would you need for ± 5%?
done_when: Bar chart of A and B with error bars.
The ± range for 30, 50, 100 and your own test set.
One sentence: is B really better than A?
topics.minimum: The simulation histogram and one sentence about it.
record: Explain the histogram like a weather forecast.

topics.title: Vectors: a list of numbers that points somewhere
topics.question: How can a computer hold 'meaning' in numbers?
topics.why: Embeddings, search and attention are all vectors. You will explain this to customers who think AI 'reads' text like a person.

learn.title: Vectors, what even are they? (3Blue1Brown, Linear Algebra chapter 1)
learn.how: Watch the video or read the text version. Hold on to one idea: a vector is an arrow and a list of numbers.

math.plain: A vector is a list of numbers, like [3, 4]. Its length is √(3² + 4²) = 5: Pythagoras, for any number of dimensions.

build: Describe 6 Acme emails with 3 numbers you choose: [money, urgency, technical], each 0 to 1.
Plot two of the dimensions as arrows.
Write length(v) with a plain loop (no numpy). Check it against np.linalg.norm.
Write add(a, b) and scale(v, k). Plot the results. What changed?
done_when: 6 hand-made vectors and an arrow plot.
One sentence on what scaling does to an arrow.
record: Show your 6 vectors and why you chose those numbers.

topics.title: Dot product and cosine: measuring 'alike'
topics.question: How do you measure that two meanings are close?
topics.why: Every vector search a customer buys ranks results with this formula. You should be able to compute it by hand.

learn.title: The Illustrated Word2vec (Jay Alammar): 'Personality Embeddings' only
learn.how: Read the first part only. It explains vectors and cosine similarity with a personality test.

learn.title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs (3Blue1Brown): 'Dot Product'
learn.how: In the text version, read only the 'Embedding', 'Direction' and 'Dot Product' parts.

math.plain: dot(a, b) multiplies matching numbers and adds them up. cosine(a, b) = dot(a, b) ÷ (length(a) × length(b)). It is 1 when two arrows point the same way, 0 when unrelated, −1 when opposite.

build: Write dot(a, b) and cosine(a, b) with loops. Check them against numpy.
Print the 6 × 6 cosine table for the given vectors as a heatmap.

math.plain: Stack all document vectors as the rows of a matrix M. Then M @ q is the dot product of q with every row, in one step. Same answer as a loop, just much faster.

build: Turn each help article into one chunk and embed them all once. Stack them into a matrix M.
